title: 3.7L Duratec Engine Component Map
introduction:
I use these exploded drawings to turn an intimidating engine into recognizable neighborhoods: the intake above, the drive components at the front, the valve gear in the cylinder heads and the lubrication hardware below. The blue components are pulled away from the gray engine so you can see their shapes and relationships. Think of it as spreading the engine's family photograph out on the bench.

Choose the view for the area you want to identify, then match a drawing's callout to the Item column in its accompanying table. Read Description for the component name and Part Number for the identifier shown. Callouts belong to their own drawing; they are not a removal sequence. Keep LH and RH labels with their named views rather than treating screen position as an engine-side label. The head views also distinguish intake from exhaust components, even where identifiers repeat.

This reference applies to the engine named above. It teaches identification and layout; it does not establish access steps, timing alignment, tightening specifications, replacement-fastener rules or replacement-part interchangeability. Once you identify a component, use its matching service procedure before dismantling anything.

edits.why: I start with the broad upper intake manifold as the visual landmark, then trace the stacked arrangement toward the lower intake manifold and engine. The drawing separates the fuel rail from its surrounding noise-shield insulators, making their different shapes easier to recognize. Use the table to distinguish the handed insulators and identify the knock sensor; an exploded position shows where a component belongs in the group, not how to reach or remove it.

edits.text: Front Cover and External Drive Components
edits.why: The large engine front cover anchors this view. Compare the crankshaft pulley and its front seal with the coolant pump and its separate pulley, then use the table to identify their associated seals and hardware. Keep the separately listed thermostat-housing O-ring seals distinct; the shared description does not make them interchangeable. The accessory-drive tensioner belongs to the external belt system. The next drawing moves behind the cover to the timing-chain components, so a familiar pulley shape should not blur those separate jobs.

I read this view by separating the chain's job from the parts that control its path. The timing chain synchronizes crankshaft and camshaft movement; the sprocket engages it, while the tensioner, tensioner arm and guides manage its running path and tension. Use the table's handed and upper/lower descriptions to distinguish the guides, and identify the channel cover plate separately. This is an identification drawing, not a timing-setting diagram: the chain's displayed shape supplies no alignment or installation instruction.

edits.text: LH Cylinder Head and Valve Gear
edits.why: Read this stack from the valve cover through the camshaft supports and camshafts to the cylinder head and its gasket. The camshafts operate the valves through the tappets; the head gasket seals the joint with the block, while the exhaust-manifold gasket belongs to a different joint. I keep the intake and exhaust labels attached to their respective camshafts, position sensors, oil-control solenoids and timing units. The solenoids control oil for variable camshaft timing; the timing units adjust the valve events, and the sensors report camshaft position. The secondary chain, tensioner and shoe form another identifiable group beside that valve gear. Use the table for quantities and identifiers, including the separately shown exhaust heat shield.

edits.text: RH Cylinder Head and Valve Gear
edits.why: Use this head's own drawing and table rather than carrying callouts across from the opposite head. The arrangement again separates the cover, camshaft supports, intake and exhaust camshafts, timing hardware, tappets and head gasket. The VCT oil-control solenoids regulate oil used to adjust camshaft timing; the VVT units make the timing adjustment, while the CMP sensors report camshaft position. I also pick out the CHT sensor—the cylinder head temperature sensor—so it is not confused with a camshaft position sensor. Similar-looking parts and repeated identifiers make the full handed and intake/exhaust descriptions especially useful here; visual resemblance alone does not establish interchangeability.

The block is the main casting supporting the cylinders and crankshaft; the detached pieces show hardware associated with its lower and rear areas. I use the keyed oil-pump entry as a starting landmark. The pump supplies oil to the lubrication passages, while the pan holds the reservoir and the screened pickup provides the pump's inlet path. Those are related jobs, not interchangeable descriptions of the same part. Match each remaining callout to its corresponding table entry before assigning a name; the rear circular components should not be identified by appearance alone. Their exploded spacing does not specify an assembly order.

I use this exploded view to connect the piston’s up-and-down movement with crankshaft rotation: the connecting rod carries the force between them. Match each drawing callout to the table’s Item column, then read its Part Number and Description, including any quantity or parent-assembly note. Above the block sits the piston and connecting rod assembly; below it are the crankshaft, curved bearing shells, main bearing caps and the support brace. The thrust washers are shown beside the crankshaft. Think of this as the bottom end’s cast photo: the shells, caps and brace crowd around the same shaft, but they are distinct parts. The spacing separates them for identification; it does not establish removal order, installation direction, bearing selection, clearances or tightening instructions.
